about: Employer callback gaps from field experiments: how much less often an employer contacts an applicant of a group than an otherwise identical applicant of the reference group. A sourced table for the employer-attitude reader (world-sale-eligibility-reads). No engine reads it yet; the gap sets totals and a per-employer spread, and never decides one employer's answer (no dice). A callback ratio is the group's callbacks over the reference group's.

black-applicants.ratioMeaning: 1 / 1.36: white applicants receive 36% more callbacks than African American applicants (studies since 1989, no change over 25 years)
black-applicants.source: Quillian, Pager, Hexel and Midtbøen 2017, PNAS 114(41), meta-analysis of 24 field experiments since 1989 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5642692/)

spreadAcrossEmployers.source: Kline, Rose and Walters 2022, QJE (NBER w29053): 108 large U.S. employers, 83,000 applications; the average gap is 2.1 percentage points fewer contacts for distinctively Black names, and the standard deviation of the gap between companies is 1.9 points; the top quintile of employers account for nearly half of lost contacts (https://causalclaims.trfetzer.com/paper/w29053.html)

spreadAcrossPlaces.note: No place-by-place study is in this table. A place's spread is the employer spread above, drawn per world; the low and high on the ratio are the studies' own range, marked ESTIMATED until a place-level source is added.

callbackRatio.boundsNote: The study's 95% confidence interval: "White applicants receive on average 24% more callbacks than Latinos (95% confidence interval of 15–33% more)." 1 / 1.33 = 0.75 and 1 / 1.15 = 0.87.

latino-applicants.ratioMeaning: 1 / 1.24: white applicants receive 24% more callbacks than Latino applicants (studies since 1989, modest evidence of a decline)
latino-applicants.source: Quillian, Pager, Hexel and Midtbøen 2017, PNAS 114(41) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5642692/)

spreadAcrossPlaces.note: Study range, not a place measure.

callbackRatio.boundsNote: Two cities; the low and high are this table's own bracket around the study, not a published interval.

black-names-resume-audit-2004.ratioMeaning: White-sounding names receive 50% more callbacks (1 / 1.5), Boston and Chicago, uniform across occupation, industry and employer size
black-names-resume-audit-2004.source: Bertrand and Mullainathan 2004, American Economic Review 94(4) (https://www.nber.org/papers/w9873)

spreadAcrossPlaces.note: Two cities; the low and high are this table's own bracket around the study, not a published interval.

older-applicants.ratioMeaning: Compared to the youngest group, middle-aged (49 to 51) applicants received 18% fewer callbacks and seniors (64 to 66) 35% fewer, in a secondary summary of the study; women 64 to 66 were called back 12% of the time against 19% for women 29 to 31, and older men showed little gap except in some jobs
older-applicants.source: Neumark, Burn and Button 2019, Journal of Political Economy. The 18% and 35% figures are from a secondary press summary, which is what was read; the paper itself (https://admin.nber.org/data-appendix/w21669/On%20line%20appendix%20for%20JPE%2010-16%20final.pdf) has not been read, so this row is ESTIMATED until it is.

spreadAcrossPlaces.note: Study range, not a place measure. The study's design has been debated (identical resumes leave older applicants with gaps in their history).

applicants-with-a-criminal-record.reference: the same applicant without a record

callbackRatio.boundsNote: One city (Milwaukee); the low and high are this table's own bracket around the study.

applicants-with-a-criminal-record.ratioMeaning: A prison record cut callbacks by 50% for white applicants and by over 60% for Black applicants; callbacks with a record were 17% (white) and 5% (Black)
applicants-with-a-criminal-record.source: Pager 2003, American Journal of Sociology 108(5), 937-975; the no-record callback rates were not confirmed here, so this row is ESTIMATED until read from the article (https://users.ssc.wisc.edu/~gwallace/Papers/Pager%20(2003).pdf)

spreadAcrossPlaces.note: One city (Milwaukee), so no place spread is claimed.
